The Mexican ground squirrel Ictidomys mexicanus is a diurnal rodent inhabiting arid and semi-arid grasslands from northern Mexico northward into the southwestern United States. Foraging primarily on seeds, green vegetation, and occasional insects, this species exhibits a life history strategy typical of many hibernating sciurids, characterized by a relatively short active season and a pronounced reliance on stored energy reserves. Comparative data from the closely related thirteen-lined ground squirrel provide a useful framework for estimating several key traits. For instance, the wet weight at birth likely approximates 3.24 grams [Wwb = 3.24 grams], a value consistent with the altricial neonatal state typical of the genus Ictidomys, where newborns are hairless, blind, and entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial weeks of postnatal development.

Adult females of Ictidomys mexicanus attain an ultimate wet weight averaging approximately 310 grams [Wwi = approximately 310 grams], although individual variation across the species range can span from a minimum of 217 grams up to 398 grams. This body mass places the species among the medium-sized ground squirrels, comparable to its congeners. The adult mass is reached after a period of rapid juvenile growth, which under typical thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] for active-season body temperature regulation, proceeds at a pace that allows females to enter their first reproductive season at a size sufficient for gestation and lactation. Growth trajectories from field studies suggest that juveniles attain near-adult mass within their first summer of life.

Female Mexican ground squirrels produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = a single litter per year], which is a common reproductive schedule among hibernating sciurids constrained by a brief growing season. Within each litter, the number of pups ranges from 1 to 10 [N_R_i = 1 to 10], yielding an annual reproductive output that can vary considerably with resource availability. This reproductive strategy balances the energetic demands of lactation, which is energetically costly, against the need to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for the subsequent winter torpor period. The timing of parturition is synchronized with the spring green-up, ensuring that peak milk demand coincides with maximum food abundance.

Gestation in Ictidomys mexicanus is a relatively short period, lasting approximately 25 days [tg = approximately 25 days] when measured at a stable body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a duration consistent with the range of 23 to 28 days reported for other small-bodied ground squirrels. Following birth, the altricial neonates remain in the subterranean nest, where they are nursed exclusively for a period of about 30 days since birth [tx = about 30 days since birth] under the same thermal conditions. This weaning age marks the point at which the young begin consuming solid food and emerge from the burrow, though they may remain associated with the mother for a short period thereafter as they learn to forage independently in the surrounding habitat.

Sexual maturity is attained approximately 365 days since birth [tp = approximately 365 days since birth] at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], meaning that most females are capable of breeding in their second calendar year, shortly after emerging from their first hibernation. This delay until the second spring reflects the time required to achieve full adult body size and deposit adequate fat stores to support the energetic costs of pregnancy and lactation. Maximum recorded longevity for this species is estimated at 8 years [am = 8 years] at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a figure derived from captive records of the congener Ictidomys tridecemlineatus. Resting metabolic rate measurements conducted during the active season at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] indicate a maximal basal oxygen consumption of 278.6 milliliters per hour [JOi = 278.6 milliliters per hour] at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], reflecting the energetic demands of maintaining homeothermy in a relatively small-bodied mammal.
